Title: Disturbing Draft Behavior at the NE Qualifier

Messages.Author: echia...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:
First off I have to give props to Josh for running a superb qualifier
this past weekend. The qualifier in Providence was among the best-run
qualifiers I have seen in years.

There was however a rather disturbing incident during the Sunday event
(which was beyond the control of the tournament organizers, who are
faultless) that I feel needs to be addressed.

On Sunday there was a booster draft event (4 Cam, 2 Anarchs, 4
Legacies). There were originally 24 people who paid the entry fee and
participated in drafting. Five of these individuals (all apparantly
from Maine) seemed to have ulterior motives however and took off
promptly after the drafting process, without playing a single game.

After talking with Josh, it seems that he was under the impression that
the Maine players were going to play in the first round before leaving.
Now I do understand that sometimes circumstances may arise forcing an
individual to leave prematurely. And it is true that the first round
did not start until around noon (the tournament was scheduled to begin
at 10 AM).

I am not sure what the experiences of the other draft tables were like,
but my table included one Maine player whose behavior was especially
egregious. Now I'm not going to be naming any names at this time, but
I'll just refer to this individual as "Person X". Although I did not
know Person X very well prior to this qualifier, I was acquainted with
him from a few other events and he generally seemed to be an okay guy.
Person X was apparantly aware that he was not going to be playing in
the draft event so he decided to participate in only the draft phase
but with the sole intention of rare drafting.

Now I know that some people will rare draft, and I'll readily admit
that I have done so on occasion as well. There's nothing intrinsically
wrong with it but the catch is that normally when you rare draft,
you're stuck playing with whatever deck you did end up drafting. So
passing on those really useful commons to get those unplayable
corner-case rares is going to come back to haunt you during the actual
rounds. But rare drafting with no intention of playing is problematic
because not only does it distort the deck-building environment of
anyone at your table but it is also extorting the other players from
what they are paying for.

At one point during the draft, Person X specifically asked aloud
whether a card (Rumors of Gehenna) was rare. Most of us didn't think
anything of it at the time, but now after seeing the behavior of the
Maine contingent, it makes a lot more sense in hindsight. But the most
offensive aspect of this entire travesty is that right before the Maine
players were about to leave, Player X was *bragging* about how he had
rare drafted and ended up with 21 rares. I kid you not. He was BRAGGING
about it.

After this issue was brought to their attention, Josh and Oscar were
quick to rectify part of the problem. At least for players at my draft
table, we each got 2 random rares from Legacies (to keep - not for
playing in the draft though). I applaud the organizers for addressing
this issue promptly and efficiently.

But I have nothing but scorn for the Maine players who would stoop to
such a low. One of the other draft participants I talked to said that
this was the sort of behavior you'd expect from Magic players and that
it's quite likely that the rare drafter(s) may try to earn a quick buck
by putting them up on eBay. I can't help but agree. In the future, I
will NEVER sit at a draft table with Person X ever again. If I was
placed in such a position, I would request to be moved to a different
draft table and if that was not possible I would rather drop from the
tournament entirely than enable his repugnant behavior. (I mean, who
knows when the guy might just "suddenly" have to leave again?).
Similarly, I will be extremely apprehensive about sitting at a draft
table with any Maine players ever again.

So I just thought that this issue needed to be brought into the open.
In addition, I would be extremely interested in hearing about the
experiences from the other draft tables.

- Eric Chiang

Well, the last sentence of the paragraph is likely the crux of the problem
right there. Two hour delays in tournament start time play hell with
peoples' travel schedules. It sounds quite likely from your description
that the players involved probably understood they couldn't play out the
tournament no matter what but entered it with the intention of drafting
for what they wanted to keep more than what they wanted to play. When
the tournament got delayed *two* *hours* (!), it probably added quite a
bit to their cynicism about the whole affair and deducted all the rest of
whatever integrity they planned to have it altogether.

I'm not going to defend what they did, but two-hour delays in tournaments,
especially on the last day, are really unacceptable and just don't help
matters.

> but with the sole intention of rare drafting.

I'm not going to defend them, exactly - but I do intend to be a bit of
an apologist for it. I think you're taking the matter more seriously
than is warranted. You have to accept that you just can't stop this
sort of thing.

1) Draft tournaments in Jyhad just aren't very good. Some people like
them, I expect, because there's still a lot of quick-on-your-feet type
nuances to work through and some games aren't absolutely hopeless. I
guess it probably depends on your attitude a lot. But a lot of us
just feel like they're an excercise in masochism anyway so why take
them seriously? (I'm not questioning why you should take them seriously,
if you like. I'm just saying a lot of people won't take them seriously
even when they choose to participate.)

2) Was there anything else to do on Sunday for VtES players who don't
like playing limited? Anything at all? A good way to avoid people
popping into limited events who really don't like them and won't take
them seriously is to provide some kind of alternative constructed event.
Even if you don't want to provide an alternative sanctioned constructed
tournament, there could be some house-rules contructed tournament. I
suspect a Rapid Thought tournament might be ideal for such a time.

3) Nothing in the entire universe can ever, EVER stop this including
making people play one game or two games or the whole tournament or
whatever***. I could do it pretty much without thinking about it if I
really had a mind to. (I can't foresee why I ever would but make no
mistake, I could.) You draft what you want and then you just grit your
teeth and you accept that you will get beaten like a red-headed
stepchild. But so what? I got the cards! Wheeeee!

(*** - except things like ante. That might help a bit. I think most
people don't really like ante, though.)

So I guess that's my answer: a combination of more acceptance of the
situation and, perhaps, a bit more awareness about avoiding certain
kinds of things that will tend to invite it.

Fred

There are a variety of ways to stop raredrafting. A major bundle of
ways involves the rares being the prizes. I played one CCG draft
where I only got to keep some of my rares. It's common for team
drafts to have the winning team get all of the rares. Can have
everyone draft rares after the event based on what position they came
in. Etc. I don't see this going over so well with a lot of casual
limited players, but who knows?

Could just have everyone keep the rares they crack, though this cuts
down on skill. Somewhat. There's much less of a penalty taking some
suboptimal cards with V:TES than, say, with Magic. So, even if there
are significant rewards for doing well in the event, the incentives
against raredrafting are limited.

I just see it being too much effort to try to counter raredrafting
given the V:TES limited player base I'm used to.

I'm not sure why it's that big of a deal from the standpoint of
disliking raredrafting that players raredrafted and then didn't play.
I mean, suppose they did play. Maybe they all get beat, but they
still have the cards they drafted. And, in fact, by not playing, they
can't get any prizes, so the non-raredrafters are compensated right
out of the gate with more cards or the opportunities for more cards.

I can certainly see other reasons to get annoyed by a bunch of players
not playing, so I fully support the rule about playing that was
quoted.

So here we have the official solution.

In general i think rare drafting is not the big problem for draft play.
1st. If i get the cards for the draft as a bargain, i will usually put
that in the prizes and not in the drafted cards. It is not so
interesting to draft five more rares, if you win 5 boosters with fifth
place.
2nd. As judge/organizer i always tell the players what card (usually
the last card) is the rare card. So everyone has the same possibility
to draft a rare card.
3rd. A good rare card is usually drafted in the first pick (Two times i
got a Powerbase Montreal with first pick. That is not rare drafting, it
is a winning card for the games.) You usually only get weak rares later
on. So why draft a weak rare, that has not much value on ebay, if i can
win the tournament?

That draft is a wonderful tournament concept doenst need to be
discussed. There may be many people who prefer constructed, there are
also many people who hate constructed because of its nature to have
overpowered decks.

But the actual draft playing is hampered by the fact that we still have
no good base to draft from. SW and CE are not so easy available, and
have some problems (all good CE vote cards are in starters for
example).. Other sets are often very limited for draft play.

It would be also very good, if the tournament rules for drafting would
be more flexible, allowing starter draft (including the cards of
starters in the draft process gives you good and cheap basic cards) or
random booster selection (including two BH boosters isnt usually enough
to play a BH deck - if every player could draft them at a different
time, you have more chance to get the BH cards you need).

Let me explain the situation from my own perspective, as the organizer
of the event. I take partial blame for what happened, and I apologize.

The person in charge of driving that group home, came up to me before
the event began.
He specifically asked me if they could draft and then leave before Round
1, as they wanted to leave earlier than expected.
I explained to him that it was *preferable* if they would play one
round; I did not directly quote the VEKN rule but I thought he got the
message. He said he would go discuss it with his fellow players, and I
assumed that they came to the decision that they would sit down for one
round. I may have been unclear, and I may have been naive, about the
situation.

After drafting was over, and I had already determined Round 1 seating
(with those players in the stack), I discovered that they were not
staying, and I witnessed this "Player X" bragging about how many rares
he had drafted, and calling himself a Drafting Pirate.

I did not demand the cards back at this time, which is my fault as a
judge. I take responsibility for that mistake and unfamiliarity with
that VEKN rule.

Oscar and I tried to resolve it in the fairest way possible, and in
the end I don't know how it had affected the actual deckbuilding ability
of the drafters present.

In hindsight, if I had known they had made their decision to leave, even
if I was going to allow them to draft out of the kindness of my heart, I
would have placed them all at the same table, with no one else, for the
drafting round, and not counted them as a part of the event.

But, due to this unfortunate incident and misunderstanding, I will deal
with this group of people privately, when it comes to future Limited
events.

Eric, I wish you had brought this up in a private discussion with myself
and the other organizers, rather than posting it to a public forum
first, but I do understand your concerns.

I would like to give those players the opportunity to contact me first,
before I contact them regarding the situation.

Yeah, as Eric said, this was *not* a two hour delay in the tournament. When
you start a draft event at 10 am, you start *drafting* at 10 am. Drafting
and deck construction takes at least an hour if everyone involved is already
an experienced drafter - two hours is not at all unreasonable with a large
draft where a number of participants haven't done a lot of drafting in their
lives.

This is why draft events are usually 2 rounds plus final rather than 3
rounds plus final: you expect to use the 2 hours that would "normally" go
into the third preliminary round for the drafting process instead.

Now, it *is* possible that they entered the tournament not understanding
this about draft - that there's an hour or two of time to invest before the
games begin.

I actually agree with that to some extent. Not with your arguments,
necessarily, but that you can't entirely stop people from rare-drafting (nor
do you really want to).

To my mind, it's pretty much up to each participant in a draft tournament to
decide how much they want to value drafting the rares from the packs they
open versus drafting the strongest card in terms of gameplay for their draft
deck. To me, each time I open a draft pack, I'm going to consider how much
I value the rare versus whatever else is in the pack. There are plenty of
crappy rares that I'm going to pass, but there are also a significant number

They don't need to be remotely comparable. They just need to give a sense

spell colors in Magic. There's also the issue of what happens when your
cards don't match your vampires, which tends to make for a very
uninteresting game.

Jyhad is going to be play-balanced completely differently than a game like
Magic for a number of reasons. I think the two most important ones are
the fact that you automatically draw a card when you play a card in Jyhad -
which makes the opportunity cost of a card different - and the fact that
there's no card limits - which makes it very difficult to just throw away
some slots on common card sheets for booster packs to cards that are ass

Magic). I suspect these things tend to make it more difficult to print
boosters that can be drafted in small, affordable numbers and yield
decks that do much.

enough that the drafting portion of the tournament makes up somewhat for
the less interesting games.

> complaining about how bad their decks were. Um, bad in comparison to
> what?

Constructed, obviously. But it's more than just an issue of comparing
limited directly to constructed. It's also what happens in a game when
you've got five bad decks going against each other. I can bleed for one
at zero stealth, get intercepted, and we hand-strike each other at one
strength. Well, that's pointless. So I don't. I sit and draw a card.
Not that I'm particularly looking forward to drawing anything in my
library...

Jyhad, with its abundant card flow is a much more combo-based game than
Magic, with its four-card limit, one draw per turn. In constructed,
obviously you build your deck carefully to include the card combinations
you want and the ones that will work with your vampires. Therefore, being
constrained to a small collection of cards, even one that you draft, is
a much worse handicap than in Magic.

Fred

> departed, which is truly poor sportsmanship. I want to actively discourage

This is the key to me. It was poor sportsmanship. Other people have
pointed out that what happened is virtually indistinguishable from some
alternative form of conduct given the same circumstance: either playing
with a horrible deck, or just showing up for the first round and
transferring out, or the fact that the only rares you're missing out on
are ones that are bad enough that a player wouldn't want to use them.
And this is why we have notions like "sportsmanship" - because there's
some behavior that we're more or less powerless to control, but we want
to discourage it for the sake of making the game more enjoyable.

If I sat down at a table and my prey said "Guess what? I'm not going
to go forward all game, I'm just going to wall up and get my .5 vp,"
and then proceeded to do so, the outcome would be identical to a game
where she just did that anyway without telling you about it beforehand.
But I would be mad. It leads to a lot of upset and anger if you feel
like someone isn't playing by the same rules as you are.

Going back to the point about mostly useless rares being the ones
plucked out - there is a whole other impact here. If the player is
drafting all rares, then the player is not drafting "power commons" -
bounce, pool gain, damaging votes ... which can lead to other
destabilizing effects, since players next to them will get that much
more of a share at these cards. One player's poor valuation of cards
will always be to the benefit of his podmates, but it makes you a
little more upset if the only reason is for something purely extrinsic
to the tournament.

> For future Limited events, I will make sure that *all* players are aware
> that drafting is disallowed without playing one round.

I encourage this. Really, I would be far less upset if Player X had
just said, at the beginning of the draft, "Hey guys, I just found out I
have to leave a little early, but I'm just going to hang around and
draft - don't worry, I'll just be taking out all the useless rares you
guys don't want anyway!" If all the differences are as negligible as
everyone says, then there should be no problem with this, and the other
players in the pod should be overjoyed that they'll have more useful
cards. I still don't like it, and it would be a violation of the VEKN
rules, but if the players aren't planning anything shady then they
shouldn't have a problem telling everyone about it. Eric mentioned
that knowledge would help change his drafting strategy. Since I only
played my first draft game ever on Saturday, I'm new enough to not have
much of a drafting strategy beyond "Me like brain and eye," so I can't
say I'd draft any differently.

What Player X (again, I don't know the others - at least one of the
other Maine players was in the Saturday evening tournament and played a
good game) did was unsportsmanlike. And he bragged about it
afterwards. When he got roundly condemned by everyone around, he tried
to laugh it off, but the people there took it seriously. It's the kind
of conduct that I don't think people should throw their hands up at and
say "It can't be stopped, just suck it up." It's the kind of things
where if people say it's poor play long enough, then people will accept
that it is. Isn't that a better gaming environment?

I'm not advocating vigilanteism or any kind of blacklist, but this
community operates on reputation in a lot of ways. I have no opinion
of "the Maine group," other than Player X, and I don't see that there's
any harm by Eric bringing a complaint about this conduct into this
forum. Everyone seems to be labelling this behavior as a necessary
evil incident to the draft format. Maybe it's why draft isn't terribly
popular in this game. But it seems desirable to me that if people feel
like a certain normative perspective would improve things, that should
be encouraged.

And condemning bad behavior, even if there's no punishment other than
general approbrium, is a positive thing. It wouldn't have been that
hard for Player X to do any number of mitigating things, starting with
returning the cards drafted when he realized he couldn't play (of
course, then don't we have to worry about people unsatisfied with their
draft getting a free refund, as it were?), or telling his pod that it
was the case (after all, we should be happy about it, right?), or even
after making his very ill-advised joke about being a drafting pirate,
walking away with 21 rares for the price of 10, just saying that he was
kidding, or being sincerely disappointed about not being able to play.

I don't see anyone that's roundly approved of what Player X did and
thinks it's a great asset to the gaming environment. I just see a lot
of people offering ex post justifications for why it's not that
harmful. But if you looked around at the faces of the people standing
there when Player X was telling everyone this, you would see the harm.

posting to the Google group concerning the Maine players. Since I'm one
of them I thought I should tell my side of the story.

from the draft and go home. One member of our group consulted with Josh

Eric Chiang wrote, "Now I know that some people will rare draft, and
I'll readily admit
that I have done so on occasion as well. There's nothing intrinsically
wrong with it but the catch is that normally when you rare draft,
you're stuck playing with whatever deck you did end up drafting. So
passing on those really useful commons to get those unplayable
corner-case rares is going to come back to haunt you during the actual
rounds."

Oh? Is this so? 10 packs = 110 cards. If you were to use all the cards
you would roughly have a 90 card deck and a full crypt. Does anyone
know people who play with a 40 card deck? Is that cheating?

Eric Chiang wrote, "At one point during the draft, Person X
specifically asked aloud

anything of it at the time, but now after seeing the behavior of the
Maine contingent, it makes a lot more sense in hindsight."

Really? I saw that card go around _twice_ and nobody took it. I already
own several copies of the card so I can't see how that was an issue. If
someone really needed it for their deck I imagine I wouldn't have seen
it twice.

Eric Chiang wrote, "But I have nothing but scorn for the Maine
players who would stoop to such a low. One of the other draft
participants I talked to said that this was the sort of behavior you'd
expect from Magic players and that it's quite likely that the rare

who drafts cards can take what they want for whatever reason they want.
Every player at a draft has to make a decision on what card to pull and
what cards to pass. If they are passing a decent card they shouldn't
expect to see it come back to them. I fail to see how this is any
different.

I'll admit, if I did do anything to other players, I perhaps managed to
help some of the people in my pod. One guy to my right seemed overjoyed
when he saw some of the stuff I was passing him. Why? Because I was
passing him utility commons instead of corner case rares. Example: he
was passed Governed the Unaligned instead of an Ankara Citadel.

NEVER sit at a draft table with Person X ever again. If I was placed in

entirely than enable his repugnant behavior."

this won't happen again. This was all a mistake. It wasn't anything
intentional, like agreeing to split a table _before_ the round even
started. It was overheard that Eric made a deal and gave the table to
his co-conspirator. That is something that is truly repugnant and
unsportsmanlike. I spoke with one player who was really frustrated when
Eric did little more than influence out vampires and then roll over for
his predator. I wish there was a way to halt this kind of vile and
repugnant behavior. I guess I can just be happy that Eric won't sit at
a table with me and will leave the tournament instead. Sometimes good
things come out of even the worst situations :)

summarize those other responses, the Maine players didn't know that

they would probably be leaving early. It was all basically a
misunderstanding.

suspect behavior by Eric Chiang. Several of the players relay the same

As I was not there, I do not know. But when I have more than a couple

fabrication. Feel free to form your own conclusions.

Here's the place I think you were in the wrong. If you drafted, you
entered a tournament. I've never heard of anyone holding a draft just
for the sake of drafting. (I suppose you could do it; I've just never
heard of it.) So you entered a tournament, period.

The primary purpose of entering a tournament is to compete with other
players and attempt to win that competition. No one should be entering
tournaments with any other primary purpose in mind. Secondary
purposes are reasonable enough: testing an experimental deck against good
compeition, occupying time, social interaction, and, yes, getting some
good rares in a draft is fine. But the expection and common (unspoken)
agreement) is that everybody is primarily trying to win the tournament
or the whole concept of tournaments as competition breaks down.

If you were entering and attempting to win the NEQ and you'd heard that
another group of players was entering for some non-competitve reason,
I think you might mind too. Let's say a bunch of guys decided they
wanted to affect NEQ tables with enough events to play Fall of the
Sabbat and Fall of the Camarilla just for the pure giggle factor - to
have fun screwing up the strategy of the other competitors. They
had no intent to compete for or win any qualifying spots, let alone
the championship of the NEQ? How would you feel about that?

It's not just an issue of breaking a rule in a technical sense or
something. And it's not about whether you were "bragging" or not.
(I respectfully disagree with Josh Feuerstein about that.) It's
really, REALLY important in a competition that all competitors be
competing at all times. It's a question of treating other game
players the way you would like to be treated.

Fred

rule. Even if they just built the deck to mess with the table but
they actually try to win with the deck just to conform to the play-
to-win rule, I still assert that's bad behavior. Some things are bad
even when they defy creating a specific rule to outlaw. (In fact,
the play-to-win rule isn't all that enforceable either because it's

intent.)

some complexity here due to the issue of multiplayer-game metagaming:
playing one game in a non-competitive manner in order to improve one's
competitive position in future games. That kind of thing is
controversial and I don't want to start a debate about it here.
But I would like to point out that everything that's game-legal
and tournament-legal isn't necessarily moral. I consider it an
unspoken tacit agreement that everyone who signs up for a tournament
is in the tournament to win the tournament or do as well as they can
during the rounds they can play. Otherwise, all the balance built
into the game - which rests on the foundation that people using the
cards are trying to win - breaks down.

Sorry. That's where I draw the line. The other competitors didn't
show up to buy decks and draft cards just so other people could jump
in and draft cards for no other purpose than to own them. It may
not be something you can stop - which is why I agree that Eric is
making too big a deal about trying to stop it. It may not be
something you can write a rule about (other than the one that's
already there). But you're never going to get me to agree that it's
OK to do.

Maybe nothing, but that's not my point. I'm just saying I don't
think you can defend the behavior.

Fred

Just so it's clear: people don't care about rare drafting in here
exactly because everyone understands that they will pass opportunities
to get a better card for their decks - they just realize that since it
will make such a small impact on overall performance because it's
sealed + draft (with 4 boosters for each player at most, sometimes
less), it's better to go for the best balance possible between getting
something to spice a sealed deck and make the best profit in terms of
card collection for the money spent. The proof to this is that I've
never seen anyone leave a Limited tournament in here before round 2.
People understand that playing at least two rounds is part of the fun,
rare drafting or not.

That said: as far as I can remember, there's more than one type of
draft suggested in the tournament rules, right? From that direct
experience (people drafting rares first all the time), I believe that a
format that allowed for Rare draft first (based on that format which
involves separate draft for crypt and library cards) would not seem too
difficult to manage (the Rare has been the last card on the booster for
years and several sets in a row after all) and would mitigate some
concerns. Not to mention it would actually make rare drafting *closer*
to the deckbuilding issue.

For example: during the Legacies pre-release, I picked the Rare card
first in all 4 boosters - not only because I knew I would want them,
but because some were also useful, such as Excellent Thirst. I was
playing Guruhi, and I was told later by a fellow player that he got an
Ananasi Vampirephile, even if he was playing Akunanse, because he was
rare drafting too as all the others. Suppose a third player got Wise
Spider and picked it, and so on. If we had opened all 4 boosters and
drafted all the Rares first - specially using the crypt card draft
method in some draft variant I saw once in the tournament rules, where
all vampires are placed in front of everyone on the table and each
chooses one - I'm sure he would get the Wise Spider, I'd take the
Ananasi Vampirephile, and the third player would get whatever Rare was
best for his deck. Everyone would be happy, with 4 Rares for the 4
boosters they had paid for, and with rares that would actually be used.
Of course, it would make counter-drafting a little more annoying
because it's made in the open, but since Rares are not usually that
good for a deck, the common/uncommon draft would compensate for that.

Note that this takes into consideration that most players involved do
not want to make the most for their money, such as being able to get
the highest number of Rares available. People do rare drafting in here
just because they feel they deserve X Rares since they paid for X
boosters. I know that this can seem a little odd a notion - why don't
you just buy X boosters for yourself instead? - but it becomes
understandable when you realise that not all players have that much
money to spend in boxes regularly, and that boosters are sold for 200%
more in here due to custom taxes, exchange rates etc. etc. I can let go
of a Rare here and there, but I won't condemn people who feel they
should get what they paid for in those conditions, as long as they
*play* the tournament. Fortunately, everyone understands that playing
is part of the fun.

Fabio "Sooner" Macedo
